payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.

parsed.text:
The graph already captures the key safeguard—do not mistake a newly appearing right-side mug for the source mug—but its fulfillment criteria are too strict about identity and too narrow about what counts as progress. In the edited image, the original light-blue mug is no longer clearly identifiable: a blurred blue shape remains on the left, while white mugs appear on both sides of the headphones. This supports uncertainty about correspondence, not a confident claim that the source mug moved. Preserve that distinction so the evaluator does not force a label from the right-side mug alone.

Refine the requested check’s partial criterion to cover any visually supported progress toward the requested relative placement of the source mug, including evidence that it moved rightward even if its final position or identity is not fully resolved. Keep complete fulfillment contingent on evidence that the source mug itself is to the right of the headphones. Make the absent criterion apply only when evidence supports that no requested movement occurred; disappearance, blur, or an unidentifiable replacement should remain unknown rather than be treated as absence. Ensure the unknown criterion is a genuine fallback after considering the support evidence, not a competing default.

The support check is useful and should remain a support-only check, with its evidence explicitly consumed by the requested check. Its current dependency is structurally appropriate. Keep the single requirement and outcome, preserve their exact source quote and text, and retain the distinction between the source mug and duplicates. Do not add a requirement for mug color, count, or other unrequested edits; those details may inform correspondence but must not become fulfillment conditions. This should improve calibration on ambiguous edits while preserving the instruction and allowing a partial judgment only when actual progress is supported.
